notes: TOP500 data scraped from top500.org list pages (/lists/top500/list/YYYY/MM/?page=1..5) and top-10 pages, cross-checked with the TOP500 performance-development series (/statistics/perfdev/), which is used for n1_rmax and n500 (more digits). All values are GFLOP/s. List pages show values rounded to 2 decimals in the page's unit, so n10/n100/rank_curve carry that rounding. Quirks: the full 11/1995 list returns 404 on top500.org (only the top 10 are available; n100 null; n500 from perf-dev); the 11/2018 list page labels values GFlop/s but shows TFlop/s (converted). Machine records use the Rmax/Rpeak/cores/power of the list where the machine had its best #1 Rmax (best_list). TOP500 system pages today often show later upgraded configurations, so they were not used for #1 values. year = installation year for early systems, otherwise the year it first reached #1 (see uncertain notes). Pre-1993 figures come from Dongarra's 'Performance of Various Computers Using Standard Linear Equations Software' (netlib, edition of 15 June 2014): Table 1 n=100 and TPP n=1000 (MFLOP/s), Table 3 Rmax highly parallel (GFLOP/s). Strassen-based Table 3 results were excluded. The latest TOP500 list found is November 2026 (68th edition); #1 is LineShine since June 2026. Power is null where TOP500 or a primary source does not give it. Costs are null unless a source gave one. Pre-1993 machines use the larger of Dongarra's TPP (n=1000) and highly parallel Rmax figures, because HPL lets n grow; each record says which.

machines.name: Cray-1
machines.system: Cray-1 (LINPACK figures measured on Cray-1S, same 12.5 ns CPU)
machines.site: Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory (serial 1, 1976 trial); NCAR (serial 3, 1977, first official customer)
machines.linpack_kind: LINPACK TPP n=1000 (Dongarra report, 15 June 2014 edition; Cray-1S, 12.5 ns)

linpack_detail.power_note: Russell (CACM 1978): 'Power consumption approximately 115 kw input for maximum memory size'; NCAR also lists 115 kW. Freon-cooled with a Freon/water heat exchange. The figure is the machine's electrical input; it is not stated to include the external refrigeration/condensing units or motor-generator losses.

machines.story: The first Cray-1 went to Los Alamos in 1976 for a six-month trial. NCAR became the first paying customer in 1977. At NCAR it did about 4.5 times the work of the CDC 7600 it joined. NCAR says it allowed big advances in modeling climate and severe storms, and it ran there for almost 12 years.
uncertain: power_kw: whether the 115 kW includes cooling plant and motor-generator losses is not stated (it most likely excludes the external refrigeration)
linpack: Dongarra's table lists Cray-1S, not the original Cray-1/1A; the CPU (12.5 ns, 160 MFLOP/s peak) is the same
TPP 110 MFLOP/s: run date not given in the report
Los Alamos exact install/acceptance date (March vs April 1976) not verified from a primary LANL page

machines.name: Cray X-MP
machines.linpack_kind: LINPACK TPP n=1000 (Dongarra report, 15 June 2014 edition; X-MP/416, 4 proc., 8.5 ns)
machines.cost: US$14.6 million for X-MP/48 + I/O subsystem, plus $3.5M SSD and $2M disks (NCAR, 1986)
machines.story: The X-MP put up to four Cray processors in one cabinet sharing memory. NCAR got an X-MP/48 in 1986 for its atmospheric research. In 1987 NCAR's Community Climate Model became the first of its models to use all four processors at once. It ran 3.7 times faster than on one processor.
uncertain: year: 1982 is the X-MP introduction (2-processor); the 4-processor X-MP/48 came in 1984; the measured X-MP/416 is a later 8.5 ns model
power_kw: no public figure found
price: the commonly quoted 'US$15 million' list price was not verified from a primary source; NCAR's 1986 contract figure is given

machines.name: Cray-2
machines.site: National Magnetic Fusion Energy Computer Center, Lawrence Livermore (first delivery, 1985)
machines.linpack_kind: LINPACK TPP n=1000 (Dongarra report, 15 June 2014 edition)
machines.story: The Cray-2 packed its circuit boards in a bath of Fluorinert liquid to carry away heat. The first one went to the U.S. magnetic fusion energy computer center at Livermore in 1985. It had more memory than any earlier Cray, so scientists could run much larger problems.
uncertain: power_kw: no primary figure found (150-200 kW appears only on an unofficial page)
site/date of first delivery taken from Wikipedia and a secondary history page, not a primary source
memory claim (256 Mword, more than all earlier Crays combined) from secondary sources

machines.name: Cray Y-MP
machines.linpack_kind: LINPACK TPP n=1000 (Dongarra report, 15 June 2014 edition)

linpack_detail.power_note: 120 kW is NCAR's listed electrical consumption for its Y-MP8/864 'Shavano' (1990-1997).

machines.story: The Y-MP had up to eight vector processors. NCAR ran a Y-MP8 named Shavano from 1990 to 1997 as its main computer. On an NCAR ocean model it set an industry record by sustaining more than 1 GFLOP/s.
uncertain: cost: no public price found
first customer (NASA Ames, per secondary sources) not verified

machines.name: NEC SX-3
machines.linpack_kind: Rmax, highly parallel LINPACK (Dongarra report, 15 June 2014 edition, Table 3); TPP n=1000 = 13.42 GFLOP/s

linpack_detail.later_model: SX-3/44R (2.5 ns): TPP 15,120 MFLOP/s, Rmax 23.2 GFLOP/s, peak 25.6 GFLOP/s

machines.story: NEC announced the SX-3 vector supercomputer in 1989 and shipped it in 1990. Its top model linked four processors for a claimed 22 GFLOP/s peak. In Dongarra's LINPACK tables the 4-processor SX-3/44 reaches 13.4 GFLOP/s on the n=1000 test.
uncertain: year: 1990 ship date from Wikipedia and a 1989 trade report, not an NEC primary source
site, power, cost and application story not verified
whether it was the fastest machine by LINPACK in 1990 is not established

machines.name: Cray C90
machines.linpack_kind: Rmax, highly parallel LINPACK (Dongarra report, 15 June 2014 edition, Table 3); TPP n=1000 = 10.78 GFLOP/s

linpack_detail.rmax_note: Table 3 also lists 20.65 GFLOP/s for a 16-proc C90 using Strassen's algorithm (rate counted with 2n^3/3 flops, so above peak); not used.
linpack_detail.power_note: 493.5 kW is NCAR's listed electrical consumption for its 16-processor C90 (in use 1997-1999), a site figure.

machines.story: The C90 was Cray Research's top vector machine of the early 1990s, with up to 16 processors. NCAR ran a 16-processor C90 for atmospheric research from 1997 to 1999.
uncertain: cost: no public price found
power_kw: site figure from NCAR, may include peripherals
year 1991 from Wikipedia
story: no specific application result verified

machines.name: Intel Touchstone Delta
machines.linpack_kind: Rmax highly parallel (Dongarra report Table 3, 15 June 2014 edition; Nmax 25,000)
machines.story: The Touchstone Delta was a research machine with 512 Intel i860 processors in a mesh. A consortium led by Caltech used it to process satellite images and to model molecules for AIDS research. It led to Intel's Paragon line.
uncertain: processors: a 1990 JPL release says 528 i860 units; Dongarra and TOP500 list 512 compute processors
power_kw, cost not found
applications from a JPL release and CHM via search summary

machines.name: CM-5
machines.story: Los Alamos used the CM-5 for large physics simulations. A Los Alamos molecular dynamics code (SPaSM) sustained about 50 GFLOP/s on the 1,024-node machine. The same work showed that simulations with more than 100 million particles had become possible. Such runs follow how materials deform and break atom by atom.
uncertain: story: 'how materials deform and break' is a general description of short-range MD use, not quoted from the sources

machines.name: Numerical Wind Tunnel
machines.story: Japan's National Aerospace Laboratory and Fujitsu built the NWT to replace much wind-tunnel testing with computer simulation. Engineers used it to compute air flow over wings, wing-body shapes and full aircraft. It sustained close to 100 GFLOP/s on a wide range of fluid dynamics programs.
uncertain: processors: TOP500 list pages show 140 cores for every NWT entry, while TOP500's own #1 summary says the 170 GFLOP/s run used an upgraded 167-processor system
rmax: TOP500 #1 summary page says 124.2 GFLOP/s for 11/1993; list page and perf-dev data say 124.0 (used)
current TOP500 system page 173279 shows a later Rmax of 191.98 GFLOP/s (not a #1 figure)

machines.name: Paragon XP/S 140
machines.story: Sandia's Paragon was the first massively parallel machine that was clearly the fastest in the world. In 1994 Sandia researchers simulated comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 hitting Jupiter on a Paragon. They predicted fireballs visible from Earth, and Hubble observations later matched the predicted plumes.
uncertain: story: the 1994 comet runs used an 1,840-processor Intel Paragon at Sandia per Crawford et al.; whether this was a partition of the XP/S 140 is not verified

machines.name: Hitachi SR2201
machines.story: The SR2201 was a distributed-memory parallel computer with 1,024 processors at the University of Tokyo. Its HARP-1E processors used pseudo vector processing to stream data past the cache. This let a RISC-based machine run vector-style scientific codes efficiently.
uncertain: rmax: TOP500 #1 summary page and current system page say 232.4 GFLOP/s; the June 1996 list page and perf-dev data say 220.4 (used)
story: specific scientific applications at the University of Tokyo not verified

machines.name: CP-PACS
machines.site: Center for Computational Sciences, University of Tsukuba
machines.story: Physicists and computer scientists at Tsukuba designed CP-PACS together for computational physics. Its main job was lattice QCD, the theory of quarks and gluons. It computed the masses of light hadrons and estimated light quark masses from first principles.

machines.name: ASCI Red
machines.story: ASCI Red was the first computer to pass 1 TFLOP/s on LINPACK. The U.S. stopped nuclear testing in 1992, so the weapons labs needed simulation instead. ASCI Red modeled the 3D physics of weapons and how stockpile parts age. It was upgraded twice and led seven TOP500 lists.

machines.name: ASCI White
machines.story: ASCI White served the U.S. stockpile stewardship program. In 2002 Livermore and Los Alamos ran the first full-system 3D simulations of a nuclear weapon explosion on it. The Livermore run used more than 1,024 processors and took 39 days.

machines.name: Earth Simulator
machines.story: Japan built the Earth Simulator to model global climate and solid-earth problems. It ran global atmosphere simulations with grid spacing near 10 km. Its LINPACK score was almost five times that of the previous #1, and it held the top spot for five lists.
uncertain: story: TOP500's summary says it ran coupled atmosphere-ocean simulations down to 10 km; only 10 km atmosphere (AFES) runs were confirmed from a JAMSTEC paper (via search summary)
power_kw: 3,200 kW appears in current TOP500 list data; power was not part of the original 2002 lists

machines.name: BlueGene/L
machines.site: Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (11/2004 entry: beta system at IBM Rochester)
machines.story: BlueGene/L used many slow, low-power processors instead of a few fast ones. It ran stockpile science at Livermore. In 2005 a team won the Gordon Bell Prize for atom-by-atom simulations of molten tantalum and uranium freezing under high pressure. The runs used up to 524 million atoms.

machines.name: Roadrunner
machines.system: Roadrunner - BladeCenter QS22/LS21 Cluster, PowerXCell 8i / Opteron
machines.story: Roadrunner was the first computer to pass 1 PFLOP/s on LINPACK. It paired AMD Opteron chips with IBM Cell processors, a relative of the PlayStation 3 chip. Its main job was nuclear weapons simulation, including how nuclear materials age. It also ran science from virus models to the distant universe, and it was retired in 2013.

machines.name: Jaguar
machines.story: Jaguar was an open-science machine at Oak Ridge. In 2009 nearly 30 research teams used it for climate, chemistry, materials, combustion and fusion work. One team ran century-long simulations of ocean and atmosphere circulation. A 2008 Gordon Bell Prize run on Jaguar simulated superconductors at 1.35 PFLOP/s.
uncertain: TOP500 system page 176544 now shows Jaguar's later upgraded configuration (Opteron 6274); per-list #1 values used instead
story details taken from ORNL/OLCF documents via search summaries, not read in full

machines.name: Tianhe-1A
machines.system: Tianhe-1A - NUDT TH MPP, X5670 2.93GHz 6C, NVIDIA GPU
machines.story: Tianhe-1A was the first Chinese system to top the TOP500. It combined 14,336 Intel Xeon processors with 7,168 NVIDIA Tesla GPUs. It was used for petroleum exploration and for simulating large aircraft designs.

machines.name: K computer
machines.system: K computer, SPARC64 VIIIfx 2.0GHz, Tofu interconnect
machines.site: RIKEN Advanced Institute for Computational Science, Kobe
machines.story: The K computer was the first system to pass 10 PFLOP/s on LINPACK. It opened to academic and industry users in 2012. That year a team won the Gordon Bell Prize on K for a trillion-particle simulation of dark matter. It was also one of the most energy-efficient systems of its time.

machines.name: Sequoia
machines.system: Sequoia - BlueGene/Q, Power BQC 16C 1.60 GHz, Custom
machines.story: Sequoia was the first system with more than one million cores. It was water cooled and served the NNSA stockpile stewardship program. Relative to peak speed it was about 90 times more power efficient than the earlier ASC Purple machine.
uncertain: year: TOP500 system page lists installation year 2011; first #1 was 06/2012 (2012 used)
TOP500 system page 177556 shows a later Rmax of 17,173.22 TFLOP/s; the #1 value 16,324.75 TFLOP/s (06/2012) is used

machines.name: Titan
machines.system: Titan - Cray XK7, Opteron 6274 16C 2.2GHz, NVIDIA K20x
machines.story: Titan paired one NVIDIA K20 GPU with each 16-core AMD CPU in 18,688 nodes. Its early projects simulated magnetic materials, combustion inside an engine, neutron flow in a nuclear reactor and long-term climate change. It helped show that GPUs could power large science machines.

machines.name: Tianhe-2
machines.system: Tianhe-2 (MilkyWay-2) - TH-IVB-FEP Cluster, Intel Xeon E5-2692 12C 2.2GHz, Intel Xeon Phi 31S1P
machines.story: Tianhe-2 led six straight TOP500 lists. Each of its 16,000 nodes had two Intel Xeon chips and three Xeon Phi coprocessors. Chinese reports say it was used for energy, bioscience, pollution control and high-speed rail design.
uncertain: name: current TOP500 database lists this system as 'Tianhe-2A' after its 2018 upgrade; system page 177999 shows the upgraded 61.44 PFLOP/s configuration, not the #1 values used here

machines.name: Sunway TaihuLight
machines.system: Sunway TaihuLight - Sunway MPP, Sunway SW26010 260C 1.45GHz
machines.story: TaihuLight used Chinese-designed SW26010 processors with 260 cores each. It won the Gordon Bell Prize two years in a row. The 2016 prize was for an atmosphere model, and the 2017 prize was for simulating the 1976 Tangshan earthquake.

machines.name: Summit
machines.system: Summit - IBM Power System AC922, IBM POWER9 22C 3.07GHz, NVIDIA Volta GV100
machines.story: Summit had 4,356 nodes, each with two POWER9 CPUs and six NVIDIA V100 GPUs. Early in the COVID-19 pandemic, Oak Ridge researchers used it to screen more than 8,000 compounds against the virus's spike protein. They found 77 candidates for lab testing.

machines.name: Fugaku
machines.system: Supercomputer Fugaku - A64FX 48C 2.2GHz, Tofu interconnect D
machines.site: RIKEN Center for Computational Science, Kobe
machines.story: Fugaku was the first #1 system built on Arm processors. During the COVID-19 pandemic RIKEN used it to simulate how droplets and aerosols spread indoors. The results supported wearing masks together with good ventilation.

machines.name: Frontier
machines.system: Frontier - HPE Cray EX235a, AMD EPYC 64C 2GHz, AMD Instinct MI250X, Slingshot-11
machines.story: Frontier was the first system to pass 1 EFLOP/s on LINPACK. Early users simulated small modular nuclear reactors to cut design time and cost. The SCREAM cloud-resolving climate model, run on Frontier, won the 2023 Gordon Bell Prize for climate modeling.
uncertain: year: TOP500 system page lists installation year 2021; first #1 was 06/2022 (2022 used)
story: reactor and SCREAM details taken from ORNL/OLCF coverage via search summaries, not read in full

machines.name: El Capitan
machines.system: El Capitan - HPE Cray EX255a, AMD 4th Gen EPYC 24C 1.8GHz, AMD Instinct MI300A, Slingshot-11
machines.story: El Capitan serves the NNSA's nuclear stockpile mission, mostly on classified work. It runs ensembles of high-resolution 3D multiphysics simulations to check the aging stockpile without nuclear tests. A sister system, Tuolumne, handles unclassified science.
uncertain: story details taken from LLNL reports via search summaries, not read in full

machines.name: LineShine
machines.system: LineShine - LingKun, LX2 304C 1.55GHz, LingQi, Kylin OS
machines.vendor: Shenzhen Cloud Computing Center Co., Ltd.
machines.story: LineShine is the first TOP500 system to pass 2 EFLOP/s using CPUs only, with 304-core LX2 processors and no GPUs. A team at Sun Yat-sen University designed it. It has supported work in atmospheric and ocean science, engineering simulation, materials science and drug discovery.
uncertain: year: TOP500 system page lists installation year 2025; first #1 was 06/2026 (2026 used)
story: applications are as stated by Shenzhen/SYSU sources; no independent verification
no TOP500 'top systems' history page exists for it yet

about.method: HPL Rmax for TOP500 systems; Dongarra's LINPACK report for earlier machines.
